In a class of 25 students: how big is the probability that two of them have their birthday on the same day? You answer such a question with a simulation, and you build every simulation the same way.

First a plan

Before you write code, you answer four questions.

QuestionFor the birthdays
What is one experiment?A group of 25 people, each with a random birthday
What does the experiment give back?True if two people have the same birthday, otherwise False
What do you count or measure?The share of experiments that gives True
How often do you repeat?10 000 times

The experiment as a function

import random

def has_duplicate(group):
    days = []
    for i in range(group):
        day = random.randint(1, 365)
        if day in days:
            return True
        days.append(day)
    return False

Every person gets a day from 1 up to and including 365. If that day is already in the list, there is a duplicate and the function stops with True. Otherwise the day goes into the list.

You check what an experiment does with random values you choose yourself. Suppose the days drawn are 40, 112, 7 and 112. At the fourth person 112 is already in the list: the function gives back True, and the rest of the group never gets its turn.

Repeating and estimating

def estimate_probability(group, repetitions):
    successes = 0
    for i in range(repetitions):
        if has_duplicate(group):
            successes = successes + 1
    return successes / repetitions

print(estimate_probability(25, 10000))

One possible output:

0.5671

So more than half of the classes have two students with the same birthday. That is much more than most people expect.

Checking with a known case

print(estimate_probability(1, 1000))
print(estimate_probability(366, 1000))

Output:

0.0
1.0

You only trust a surprising result once the simulation is right for cases whose answer you know. One person can't share a birthday: the probability has to be 0. With 366 people and 365 days a duplicate is unavoidable: the probability has to be 1. If your simulation gives something else there, it contains an error.

Repeating until it succeeds

def rolls_until_six():
    count = 0
    roll = 0
    while roll != 6:
        roll = random.randint(1, 6)
        count = count + 1
    return count

def average_rolls(repetitions):
    total = 0
    for i in range(repetitions):
        total = total + rolls_until_six()
    return total / repetitions

print(rolls_until_six())
print(average_rolls(10000))

One possible output:

3
6.0187

An experiment doesn't have to give back True or False. Here the outcome is a number: the number of rolls until the first six. How many rolls that will be is not fixed, so the experiment is a while.

Of such an experiment you don't estimate a probability but an average: you add up the outcomes and divide by the number of repetitions. On average you need about 6 rolls.

Drawing without putting back, such as cards from a deck, you do with card = random.choice(deck) followed by deck.remove(card).

An experiment, a repetition and a check: with those you turn a story with randomness into a number you can trust.
docs.title: From situation to simulation

docs.body:
Not everything is a line. Counts per month or per outcome you show with bars, and how a large series of measurements is spread, you see in a histogram.

A bar chart

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"]
sales = [120, 95, 140, 160]
plt.bar(months, sales)
plt.ylabel("items sold")
plt.show()

plt.bar gets two lists of equal length: the first says where each bar stands, the second how high it is. The first list can hold names or numbers. There are four bars here, and the one for April is the highest.

A histogram

scores = [3, 12, 14, 25, 27, 28, 8]
plt.hist(scores, bins=[0, 10, 20, 30])
plt.xlabel("score out of 30")
plt.ylabel("number of students")
plt.show()

plt.hist gets the raw values and does the counting itself. With bins=[0, 10, 20, 30] you give the limits of the classes: from 0 to 10, from 10 to 20 and from 20 to 30. In the first class fall 3 and 8, in the second 12 and 14, in the third 25, 27 and 28. So the bars become 2, 2 and 3 high.

You can also give bins a number: bins=20 divides the range between the smallest and the largest value into 20 classes of equal width.

Bar chart or histogram?

Use a bar chart when you already have the counts: the sales per month, or a list of counters. Use a histogram when you have a long list of separate values and want to see where most of them lie: the height of 200 students, the outcome of 2000 experiments.

Don't give a list of counters to plt.hist. The histogram then counts how often each counter occurs, and that is something very different from what the counters themselves say.

Making a simulation visible

import random

def two_dice():
    return random.randint(1, 6) + random.randint(1, 6)

counts = []
for i in range(13):
    counts.append(0)
for i in range(6000):
    total = two_dice()
    counts[total] += 1

totals = []
for total in range(2, 13):
    totals.append(total)
plt.bar(totals, counts[2:])
plt.xlabel("total of two dice")
plt.ylabel("number of times")
plt.show()

The counters are already counted, so this is a bar chart. Positions 0 and 1 of the list are never used: the slice counts[2:] leaves them out, so that there are eleven heights for the eleven totals from 2 up to and including 12. The bars form a triangle with its top at 7.

def walk(steps):
    position = 0
    for i in range(steps):
        position += random.choice([-1, 1])
    return position

end_positions = []
for i in range(2000):
    end_positions.append(walk(100))
plt.hist(end_positions, bins=20)
plt.xlabel("end position after 100 steps")
plt.ylabel("number of walks")
plt.show()

Here you have 2000 separate outcomes, so a histogram. The experiment stays a function that gives back one value; the main script repeats it, collects the outcomes in a list and draws. The histogram shows a hill around 0: most walks end close to the starting point, and the farther away, the rarer.

That is how you see in one picture what thousands of repetitions of an experiment produce.

Bisection traps a zero. There is a second way of searching: start with an estimate and improve it, again and again, until it no longer changes.

The square root according to Heron

x = 2
x = (x + 16 / x) / 2
print(x)
x = (x + 16 / x) / 2
print(x)

Output:

5.0
4.1

You are looking for the square root of 16 and guess 2. If the estimate is too small, 16 divided by the estimate is too large: 16 / 2 = 8. The real root lies in between, so you take the average of the two: 5. Then the same with 5: the average of 5 and 3.2 is 4.1. Every step is closer to 4.

Improving until it is stable

def square_root(a, tolerance):
    old = a
    new = (old + a / old) / 2
    while abs(new - old) > tolerance:
        old = new
        new = (old + a / old) / 2
    return new

print(square_root(2, 0.000001))

Output:

1.414213562373095

There is no interval here that gets narrower. You stop when two successive estimates differ by less than the tolerance. That is why the loop keeps two variables: the previous estimate and the new one. If you compare an estimate with itself, the loop stops at once.

The slope of a function

def slope(f, x):
    h = 0.0001
    return (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h

def f(x):
    return x ** 3 - x - 1

print(round(slope(f, 2), 2))

Output:

11.0

You approximate the slope at a point by taking a very small step h sideways and looking at how much the function rises: the difference in function value divided by h. You don't need derivative rules for it, only the function itself.

A Newton step

x = 2
x = x - f(x) / slope(f, x)
print(round(x, 3))

Output:

1.545

Newton follows the tangent line. At the estimate x = 2 the function value is 5 and the slope is 11. If you walk down along that straight line, you reach the axis 5 / 11 further to the left. That point is the next estimate: x - f(x) / slope.

def newton(f, start, tolerance):
    old = start
    new = old - f(old) / slope(f, old)
    steps = 1
    while abs(new - old) > tolerance:
        old = new
        new = old - f(old) / slope(f, old)
        steps += 1
    return new, steps

solution, steps = newton(f, 2, 0.000001)
print(round(solution, 4), steps)

Output:

1.3247 6

The loop is Heron's, with a different rule for improving. It also counts its steps and gives them back together with the solution.

Fast, but not without risk

From 1 to 2, bisection needs twenty steps to get to within a millionth: every step gains a factor of 2. Newton and Heron roughly double the number of correct digits per step and are there after a handful of steps.

Newton can fail. Where the graph runs flat, the slope is almost zero: the division then gives a huge jump and the next estimate lands far away, sometimes at another zero. That can't happen to bisection once it has a sign change.

Choose bisection when you want certainty and know a sign change. Choose Newton when you have a good start value and speed matters.

An estimate, a rule for improving it and a stop condition: a search method needs nothing more.

With the turtle module you draw by steering a turtle across the screen. It carries out every instruction you give — forward, turn, pen up — straight away, and wherever it walks with its pen down, a line appears.

Creating a turtle

A turtle script always starts the same way: you bring in the module with import turtle and then create a turtle that you give a name, for example t. After that you give all drawing instructions to t, with a dot in between.

import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
t.forward(100)
turtle.done()

This draws a straight line of 100 steps. The last line, turtle.done(), belongs at the bottom of every turtle script: it makes sure the turtle window stays open properly when the drawing is finished.

The turtle window appears by itself, but doesn't close by itself: you do that yourself by closing the window when you have finished looking.

The basic commands

CommandWhat it does
t.forward(100)walk 100 steps forward
t.backward(50)walk 50 steps backward
t.left(90)turn 90 degrees to the left
t.right(90)turn 90 degrees to the right
t.penup()pen up: move without drawing
t.pendown()pen down again
t.pencolor("red")draw in red from now on

Important: t.left(90) turns from the direction the turtle is facing, not from yours. If it turns left twice in a row, it then faces the other way. If you want to predict what a script draws, follow the turtle step by step and keep track of which way it is facing.

So this script draws a square — four times the same thing: walk one side and make a quarter turn.

import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
t.forward(100)
t.left(90)
t.forward(100)
t.left(90)
t.forward(100)
t.left(90)
t.forward(100)
t.left(90)
turtle.done()

Decisions in a drawing

Everything you know about conditions works here too. Here the user's input decides which color is used for drawing:

import turtle

color = input("red or blue? ")
t = turtle.Turtle()
if color == "red":
    t.pencolor("red")
else:
    t.pencolor("blue")
t.forward(100)
turtle.done()

In the same way, a condition can decide which shape appears, or how big it gets — the if/elif/else chains from the previous lessons then simply control drawing instructions instead of print.

With that, you can program a drawing that reacts to what the user types.

A program that gives the right answer once is not correct just because of that. Testing is systematically trying out different inputs — test cases — to check that the program does what the task asks in every case.

Choosing test cases

Trying one ordinary case and being satisfied: that is the trap. A good set of test cases covers three kinds:

  • Ordinary cases — input as you expect it, for example 7 for "enter a number".
  • Edge cases — values exactly on a boundary. If your program checks number >= 10, test with exactly 10: that is where the difference between > and >= is.
  • Special cases — 0, negative numbers, equal values. That is exactly where errors turn up that you never see with ordinary input.

Predict first, then run

A test case only really works if you write down in advance what the output should be, and only then run the program. If something different comes out than you predicted, you have found an error — either in the program, or in your own understanding of it. Both are valuable.

a = int(input("First number: "))
b = int(input("Second number: "))
print("Average:", a + b / 2)

Prediction for the input 4 and 6: the average is 5. Actual output:

Average: 7.0

The difference gives the error away: because of the order of operations, Python calculates a + (b / 2). The fix is (a + b) / 2. Without a prediction, 7.0 might simply have been believed.

Three kinds of errors

When something goes wrong, it helps to recognize which kind of error you are dealing with.

  • A syntax error: the script doesn't even start. Python reports SyntaxError, for example for a forgotten colon after an if.
  • A runtime error: the script starts, but crashes along the way — like the ValueError when int() gets the text abc.
  • A logic error: the script runs without errors, but the answer is wrong — like the average above. You only find these by testing.

With an error message, it pays to start at the bottom: the last line names the kind of error and the reason, the lines above it point to the line number where it went wrong. Read that information first, before you start searching in the code.

Does your fix really change something? After every change, run the same test cases again — including the cases that were right at first, because a fix in one place can break something else.

With that, you can check for every program you write whether it is correct, and search in a targeted way where it isn't.

A die, a coin, a card from a deck: with the module random you let Python make such random choices. Every time you run the script, the outcome can be different.

A whole number

import random

roll = random.randint(1, 6)
print(roll)

One possible output:

5

random.randint(1, 6) gives a whole number from 1 up to and including 6. Both limits are included: unlike with range(1, 6), the 6 can come up. You import the module like math and turtle.

A decimal number or a choice from a list

print(random.random())
print(random.choice(["heads", "tails"]))

One possible output:

0.6229016948897019
tails

random.random() gives a decimal number from 0 to 1: 0.0 can occur, 1.0 never. random.choice picks a random element from a list.

What can appear?

a = random.randint(1, 3)
b = random.randint(1, 3)
print(a + b)

What this script shows, you can't predict. What it can show, you can: every whole number from 2 up to and including 6. A 1 or a 7 is impossible. That is how you look at every script with randomness: you don't ask what the output is, but which output is possible.

An event with a given probability

if random.random() < 0.3:
    print("rain")
else:
    print("dry")

One possible output:

dry

In 30 percent of the cases random.random() is below 0.3. So the condition is true with a probability of 30 percent. If you turn the sign around to >, it is true in 70 percent of the cases.

One roll, one variable

if random.randint(1, 6) == 6:
    print("six")
elif random.randint(1, 6) == 5:
    print("five")
else:
    print("something else")

This script rolls twice. Every call of random.randint produces a new number, so the second condition tests a different roll than the first. Store the roll in a variable first, as in the first example, and then test that variable.

A function with randomness

def roll_die():
    return random.randint(1, 6)

def two_dice():
    return roll_die() + roll_die()

print(two_dice())

One possible output:

8

A function that uses random gives back a new value at every call, even when it has no parameters. That is the exception to what you saw with functions: the same call, yet a different result.

roll_die() + roll_die() is two rolls. 2 * roll_die() is one roll that is doubled, so it can never be odd.

With that you can act out every game of chance and every random process in code.

A walker takes one step every second, to the left or to the right, and lets a coin decide. Such a random walk is the simplest model for everything that changes in small random steps: a speck in water, the money of a gambler, a share price.

A walk on a line

import random

def walk(steps):
    position = 0
    for i in range(steps):
        position = position + random.choice([-1, 1])
    return position

print(walk(100))

One possible output:

8

The position starts at 0 and goes one up or one down at every step. After 100 steps the walker can be at 100 or -100 at most, but usually he is much closer to 0.

Some positions are impossible. After an even number of steps the position is always even, after an odd number always odd. So after 3 steps only -3, -1, 1 and 3 are possible.

Keeping the path

def walk_with_path(steps):
    position = 0
    path = [position]
    for i in range(steps):
        position = position + random.choice([-1, 1])
        path.append(position)
    return path

print(walk_with_path(10))

One possible output:

[0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -1, 0]

The list starts with the start position and gets one more element after every step: 10 steps give 11 positions. With max(path) and min(path) you see how far the walk got.

Stopping at a limit

def play_until_end(money, goal):
    while 0 < money and money < goal:
        money = money + random.choice([-1, 1])
    return money

print(play_until_end(5, 10))

One possible output:

0

A player starts with 5 euros and wins or loses 1 euro every round. He stops when he is broke or reaches his goal of 10 euros. The number of steps is not fixed, so this is a while: the walk goes on as long as the money is between the two limits. The function gives back 0 or 10.

One walk says little

def average_position(steps, repetitions):
    total = 0
    for i in range(repetitions):
        total = total + walk(steps)
    return total / repetitions

def average_distance(steps, repetitions):
    total = 0
    for i in range(repetitions):
        total = total + abs(walk(steps))
    return total / repetitions

print(average_position(100, 2000))
print(average_distance(100, 2000))
print(average_distance(400, 2000))

One possible output:

-0.132
8.01
15.713

abs(x) gives the absolute value of x: the distance to 0, without a sign.

The average end position is around 0, because walks that end on the left and walks that end on the right cancel each other out. With the distance nothing cancels: -8 and 8 both count as 8. That is why the average distance is not zero, and it grows with the number of steps. It does grow more slowly than the number of steps itself: four times as many steps gives about double the distance.

One walk can happen to end far away or exactly at 0. Only when you repeat many of them do you see what a walk typically does.

Drawing a walk

import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
for i in range(200):
    t.left(random.choice([0, 90, 180, 270]))
    t.forward(10)
turtle.done()

In the plane the turtle chooses one of the four directions at every step and then goes 10 forward.

With a position, a random step and a loop you act out every process that is pushed along by chance step by step.

A tuple looks like a list, with one big difference: once it is made, it doesn't change any more. You use it for data that belongs together and is fixed, such as a point or a color.

Making a tuple

You write a tuple with parentheses instead of square brackets. Indexes, slices, len(), in and a for loop work as with a list.

point = (3, 5)
color = (255, 128, 0)
print(point[0])
print(len(color))

Output:

3
3

Actually the comma makes the tuple, not the parentheses: (5) is just the number 5, (5,) is a tuple with one element.

You don't change a tuple

point[0] = 10

Output:

TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

A tuple also has no append, remove or sort. If you want a different point, you make a new tuple: point = (10, 5).

A string behaves the same way. You can get a character with word[0], but word[0] = "m" gives the same kind of error.

Tuple or list?

Choose a tuple when every position has a fixed meaning and the number of elements is fixed: a point (x, y), a color (red, green, blue), a date (day, month, year). A point with three numbers is no longer a point.

Choose a list when it is a collection that can grow or shrink: the scores of a class, the names on a waiting list. That a tuple can't change also protects you: nobody can accidentally overwrite the x of a point.

Unpacking

You can give the values of a tuple to separate variables in one go. The number of names on the left has to be equal to the number of values.

x, y = point
print(x)
print(y)

Output:

3
5

That lets you swap two values without a temporary variable. Python first makes the tuple (b, a) on the right with the old values, and then unpacks it.

a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

Output:

2 1

That also works for elements of a list: colors[0], colors[2] = colors[2], colors[0].

A list of tuples

A list of points is a list in which every element is a tuple. In the for loop you unpack each point straight away:

points = [(0, 0), (100, 0), (100, 50)]
for x, y in points:
    print("x =", x, "y =", y)

Output:

x = 0 y = 0
x = 100 y = 0
x = 100 y = 50

Two names, one list

With lists, which can change, there is something to watch out for:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)

Output:

[1, 2, 3, 4]

b = a doesn't make a copy. They are two names for the same list, like two labels on the same box. What you change through b, you also see through a. You make a real copy with a slice over the whole list: b = a[:].

With tuples and strings this can't cause surprises: what can't change can't change through another name either.

With tuples you now have a way to keep data together that has to stay fixed.
docs.title: Tuples and immutability

With print() you show something on the screen. Whatever is between the parentheses appears as output when you run the script. You don't see the source code itself — only what print passes on.

Showing text

You put text between quotation marks. Python calls a piece of text like that a string. Single and double quotation marks both work, as long as you use the same kind to start and to end.

print("Hello world")
print('Goodbye')

Output:

Hello world
Goodbye

Notice: the quotation marks do not appear in the output. They belong to the source code and tell Python "this is text".

Showing numbers

For numbers you use no quotation marks. A number is not text.

print(42)
print(3.14)

Output:

42
3.14

If you write print(hello) without quotation marks, Python thinks hello is the name of something you made earlier. If that name doesn't exist, you get a NameError. So quotation marks are not optional decoration — they make the difference between text and a name.

Several values at once

If you want to show several things on one line, you can separate them with a comma inside one print call. Python then automatically puts a space between the pieces.

print("Score:", 5)
print("The sum is", 3, "+", 4)

Output:

Score: 5
The sum is 3 + 4

You can see that the commas in the source code are not in the output; they are replaced by spaces.

Comma versus plus

There is also a way to glue text together with a +. An important difference: + only works between two strings, and it adds no space.

print("Hello" + "world")
print("Hello", "world")

Output:

Helloworld
Hello world

With + you can't combine text and a number. print("score: " + 5) gives a TypeError, because + between a string and a number doesn't know what to do — add or glue? If you want to show text and a number together, use the comma form: print("score:", 5).

With that, you can type your first script of your own and see what appears on the screen.

A variable is a name you link to a value, so that you can call up that value later simply by using the name. That way you don't have to type the same text or the same number again every time, and you can keep values during a script.

Assigning with =

You link a value to a name with the equals sign. The name goes on the left, the value on the right.

name = "Mira"
age = 16
print(name)
print(age)

Output:

Mira
16

Read = as "becomes". So it is not a mathematical equality, but an instruction with a direction: from right to left.

Using the variable

Once a variable exists, you can use it anywhere you would otherwise type the value itself — in print, or together with other values.

name = "Mira"
print("Hello", name)

Output:

Hello Mira

Watch the difference between name and "name". Without quotation marks, name refers to the value you stored. With quotation marks, it is just the text name.

name = "Mira"
print("name")
print(name)

Output:

name
Mira

Overwriting a value

A variable can get a new value when you assign something to it again. The old value is then gone.

x = 10
x = 20
print(x)

Output:

20

The new value can also depend on the old one. Python then first looks at what is on the right, and only then puts the result into the name on the left.

x = 10
x = x + 1
print(x)

Output:

11

So the line x = x + 1 means: take the current value of x (10), add 1 to it, and store that result as the new x.

Rules for names

Not every piece of text works as a variable name. Python has a few rules:

  • A name starts with a letter or an underscore, not with a digit. score and _score are allowed, 2score is not.
  • A name contains only letters, digits and underscores. No hyphen, no space. my_score is allowed, my-score and my score are not.
  • A name can't be a Python keyword, such as for or if.
  • Capital letters count: name and Name are two different variables.

Text or number

The quotation marks decide the type of the value. "16" is text that happens to consist of digits. 16 without quotation marks is a number you can calculate with.

a = "16"
b = 16

They look the same on the screen when you print them, but Python treats them differently.

In Belgium you write decimal numbers with a comma, but Python expects a point. pi = 3,14 is not a decimal number — Python reads it as two separate values in a row and puts them into pi as a pair. If you want 3,14 as a number, write pi = 3.14.

A program often has to check something: is a number greater than zero? Are two values equal? You ask questions like that in Python with a comparison, and the answer is always True or False.

The comparison operators

Python has six operators to compare values:

OperatorMeaning
==is equal to
!=is not equal to
<is less than
>is greater than
<=is less than or equal to
>=is greater than or equal to

A comparison is an expression, just like 2 + 3. Python works it out to a value — only that value is not a number, but True or False.

print(5 > 3)
print(5 == 3)
print(5 != 3)

Output:

True
False
True

Watch the capital letters: Python only knows True and False. If you write true or false, Python thinks you mean a variable with that name.

Storing the answer

Because a comparison simply produces a value, you can put that answer in a variable. Python first works out the right side, and then stores the result.

age = 17
can_vote = age >= 18
print(can_vote)

Output:

False

The variable can_vote now holds the value False — not the comparison itself.

From sentence to comparison

In a task, a condition is usually written in words. Translating it to Python then means choosing the right operator: "at least" becomes >=, "at most" becomes <=, "differs from" becomes !=. The sentence "the temperature is at least 20 degrees" becomes:

temperature = 23
print(temperature >= 20)

Output:

True

Look carefully at the boundary case: with "at least 20", 20 itself is included (>=); with "more than 20", it is not (>). Exactly on the boundary, that makes the difference between True and False.

= or ==

One equals sign and two equals signs do something completely different. x = 5 is an instruction: put the value 5 in x. x == 5 is a question: is x equal to 5? The instruction stores something, the question produces True or False.

x = 5
print(x == 5)
print(x == 6)

Output:

True
False

A string and a number are never equal, even if they look the same: "5" == 5 gives False. Think of input() — it always gives back a string. If you want to compare input with a number, convert it first with int() or float().

With that, you can turn any condition in words into a comparison, and predict whether Python answers it with True or False.
docs.title: Comparisons and booleans

A rule from math, a formula from physics, a cost function from economics: you write them directly as a Python function. After that you let the computer work out the function for many values, and you search those values for what you want to know.

From formula to function

The rule f(x) = x² - 4x + 3 becomes:

def f(x):
    return x ** 2 - 4 * x + 3

print(f(0))
print(f(2))

Output:

3
-1

Math notation is not Python. Write 4 * x and not 4x, x ** 2 and not x^2, and def f(x): with return instead of f(x) = ....

A formula with several quantities gets several parameters. A capital that is invested for a number of years grows to the capital times (1 + interest rate) to the power of the number of years:

def final_capital(capital, rate, years):
    return capital * (1 + rate) ** years

print(round(final_capital(1000, 0.02, 10), 2))

Output:

1218.99

With round(value, 2) you round to two digits after the decimal point.

The math module

Square roots, the number pi and trigonometric functions are in the module math. You import it like turtle and put the module name in front of what you use.

import math

def hypotenuse(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(a ** 2 + b ** 2)

def circumference(radius):
    return 2 * math.pi * radius

print(hypotenuse(3, 4))
print(round(circumference(10), 2))

Output:

5.0
62.83

math.sin and math.cos work in radians, not in degrees.

A table of values

for x in range(0, 5):
    print(x, f(x))

Output:

0 3
1 0
2 -1
3 0
4 3

range(0, 5) produces 0 up to and including 4: the table has five rows and the 5 itself is not part of it. If you want to use the values again later, you store them in a list with append instead of printing them.

range only knows whole numbers. For a finer table you let the loop count the rows and work out x yourself: the start value plus the row number times the step.

start = 0
step = 0.5
for i in range(5):
    x = start + i * step
    print(x, f(x))

Output:

0.0 3.0
0.5 1.25
1.0 0.0
1.5 -0.75
2.0 -1.0

Here i runs from 0 up to and including 4, so x from 0 up to and including 2. Four steps of 0.5 give five rows: always one row more than there are steps.

Searching in function values

Where is f smallest? That is the pattern of finding the smallest element, now applied to function values:

smallest_x = 0
for i in range(17):
    x = i * 0.25
    if f(x) < f(smallest_x):
        smallest_x = x
print(smallest_x, f(smallest_x))

Output:

2.0 -1.0

You find a zero between two x values where the function changes sign: one function value is positive, the other negative. Their product is then negative.

def g(x):
    return x ** 3 - x - 1

for i in range(8):
    left = i * 0.25
    right = left + 0.25
    if g(left) * g(right) < 0:
        print("sign change between", left, "and", right)

Output:

sign change between 1.25 and 1.5

The step decides what you see

def h(x):
    return (x - 1.25) * (x - 1.75)

print(h(1), h(2))
print(h(1.5))

Output:

0.1875 0.1875
-0.0625

A table only shows the points you work out. With step 1, h is positive in both neighboring points: no sign change, so no zero found. Yet the function dips below zero between 1 and 2; it has two zeros and its minimum there. A step that is too big simply steps over them.

A smaller step finds more, but takes more calculating, and a table never gives you certainty that you are missing nothing.

That is how you use the computer to investigate a function of which you only know the rule.

docs.description: You can draw the graph of a function by building a list of x values and a list of function values with a loop, predict how many points are drawn, explain why more points give a smoother curve, and compare two functions in one figure.
docs.title: The graph of a function

docs.description: You can write and call your own functions: give code a name with def, pass data in through parameters, give back a result with return, predict which variables exist inside and outside a function, translate formulas from math, physics and economics into functions and make tables of values with them, and split a bigger problem into functions that call each other.
docs.title: Functions

docs.description: You can split a bigger problem into functions that each have one task, write functions that call other functions or work with lists, and test a function with well-chosen calls.
docs.title: Splitting a problem into functions

docs.description: You can use def to write a function that takes in a value through a parameter and gives back a result with return, call it, and store the result, print it or use it further in an expression.
docs.title: Writing and calling a function

docs.description: You can write a loop inside a loop to go through pairs from a list, predict how often the inner loop runs, and loop through and change a grid as a list of lists with grid[r][c].
docs.title: Nested loops and lists of lists

docs.description: You can give a graph a title and axis labels with units, draw several lines in one figure with a legend, set color and grid, and predict what a script does and does not put in the figure.
docs.title: Making a graph readable

docs.description: You can make data and functions visible with matplotlib: draw a line graph or a scatter plot from two lists, make a graph readable with a title, axis labels and a legend, build the graph of a function from a table of values you made yourself, show the outcomes of a count or simulation in a bar chart or histogram, and use numpy to calculate on a whole series of values at once.
docs.title: Making graphs

docs.description: You can write a for loop with range to repeat an operation a fixed number of times, predict the output of such a loop, build up a result in a variable, and draw regular shapes with turtle.
docs.title: Repeating with for and range

docs.description: You can write a while loop that repeats as long as a condition is true, predict when such a loop stops, recognize infinite loops, and use a loop to validate input.
docs.title: Repeating with while

docs.description: You can implement repetition with for and while, test and debug programs systematically with different test cases, and translate more complex problems into working Python code, including turtle drawings.
docs.title: Programming repetition with loops

docs.description: You can use input() to ask the user for a value with a clear prompt, store the result in a variable, and convert the input to int or float when you need to calculate with it.
docs.title: Input with input

docs.description: You can repeat a random experiment many times, count how often an event occurs and so estimate its probability, keep track of how often each outcome comes up, and explain why more repetitions give a more reliable estimate.
docs.title: Estimating a probability by repeating

docs.description: You can combine the building blocks covered so far — input, variables, calculations, print — into a small, working Python script that solves a problem described in plain language, and you can read, trace and debug such a script.
docs.title: Putting together a small script

docs.description: You can make a list grow and shrink with append, insert, remove and pop, check with in whether a value is in it, and use sum, min, max and sort.
docs.title: Changing lists with methods

docs.description: You can use a for loop to process every element of a list or string, choose between a loop over the elements and a loop over the indexes, build a new list by filtering or transforming, and draw with turtle based on a list.
docs.title: Looping over lists and strings

docs.description: You can create a list, get and change elements by their index (including a negative one), take out a part with slicing, and index a string the same way, as a sequence of characters.
docs.title: Lists, strings and indexes

docs.description: You can store data in lists and tuples: get and change elements by their index or with slicing, loop over lists and strings, write classic list algorithms yourself, make use of the difference between mutable lists and immutable tuples, and work with nested loops on pairs and grids.
docs.title: Lists and tuples

docs.description: You can write common algorithms over a list yourself: find the largest or smallest element without max() or min(), count what meets a condition, search whether and where a value occurs, and swap two elements.
docs.title: Classic list patterns

docs.description: You can predict which variables exist inside and outside a function, what happens to a variable from outside when the function assigns a value to a variable with the same name, and explain why a function should get its data through parameters and give it back through return.
docs.title: Local variables

docs.description: You can make random points inside a rectangle, check whether a point is inside a shape, and estimate the area of that shape from the share of hits, such as a circle or the area under a graph.
docs.title: Estimating an area with random points

docs.description: You can give a function several parameters, call it with the right arguments in the right order, predict which value each parameter gets, and generalize a calculation you need more than once into a function.
docs.title: Parameters and arguments

docs.description: You can translate a problem from science or economics into an equation f(x) = 0, find an interval with a sign change using a table of values or a graph, solve the equation with a search method, and check the solution by filling it in and showing it on the graph.
docs.title: From problem to zero

docs.description: You can break a more complex problem down into steps and translate it into a working Python program that combines conditions, loops and possibly turtle, and find and fix logic errors in it.
docs.title: From problem to program

docs.description: You can write and evaluate arithmetic expressions with the standard operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, **), apply the order of operations, and recognize the difference between int and float.
docs.title: Calculating with numbers

docs.description: You can make a series of evenly spaced x values with np.linspace, calculate on a whole array at once with a formula instead of a loop, use np.sin, np.cos and np.sqrt, predict where an array behaves differently from a list, and so draw the graph of a function in a few lines.
docs.title: Faster with numpy

docs.description: You can predict what goes wrong when a function prints instead of giving back a value and fix that, predict that a function stops at the first return, write functions that give back True or False, and recognize when a function does something, such as drawing, instead of calculating something.
docs.title: A closer look at return

docs.description: You can translate a described situation with randomness into a simulation: decide what one experiment is, write that experiment as a function, repeat it many times to estimate a probability or an average, and check the simulation with a case whose answer you know.
docs.title: From situation to simulation

docs.description: You can show counts per category or per outcome in a bar chart, show how a list of values is spread in a histogram, predict how high the bars become, and collect the outcomes of a simulation and make them visible.
docs.title: Bar chart and histogram

docs.description: You can search for a solution by improving an estimate repeatedly: approximate a square root with Heron's method, approximate the slope of a function numerically, carry out a Newton step, stop when two successive estimates are close enough together, and explain when such a method is faster than bisection and when it fails.
docs.title: Improving an estimate step by step

docs.description: You can program a drawing with the turtle module: create a turtle, move and turn it, set the pen and the color, and use conditions to decide what gets drawn.
docs.title: Drawing with turtle

docs.description: You can test a program systematically by trying out different test cases, choose meaningful test cases including edge cases, interpret error messages, and find and fix errors.
docs.title: Testing and debugging

docs.description: You can bring randomness into a program with the random module and use it to act out experiments: make random values, estimate a probability by repeating an experiment many times, estimate an area with random points, program a random walk, and translate a described situation into a simulation that you check with a case whose answer you know.
docs.title: Randomness and simulation

docs.description: You can make random values with the random module: a whole number between two limits, a decimal number between 0 and 1 or a random element from a list, make an event happen with a given probability, and predict which output of such a script is possible.
docs.title: Making random numbers

docs.description: You can program a random walk in which a position changes randomly at every step, keep the path in a list, make a walk stop at a limit, and explain what many repeated walks show that one walk does not.
docs.title: Random walks

docs.description: You can create, index and unpack tuples (also to swap values or to loop over a list of pairs), explain why tuples and strings can't be changed, and predict what happens when two names refer to the same list.
docs.title: Tuples and immutability

docs.description: You can use print() to show strings and numbers on the screen, and you recognize the difference between what is in the source code and what appears as output.
docs.title: Output with print

docs.description: You can assign a value to a variable with =, choose a valid name, use the variable in expressions and in print, and reassign its value.
docs.title: Variables

docs.description: You can use comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) to write expressions that give True or False, store that result in a variable, and predict what a comparison gives.
docs.title: Comparisons and booleans

docs.description: You can solve an equation for which no formula exists numerically: compare decimal numbers with a tolerance, trap and find a zero with bisection, pass a function as an argument so that one solver function works for every equation, improve an estimate step by step with the methods of Heron and Newton, make the steps of such a search visible with matplotlib, and translate a problem from science or economics into the search for a zero.
docs.title: Solving equations by searching

docs.description: You can translate a rule from math, physics or economics into a Python function, use the math module, make a table of values with a loop, and work out something about the function from those values, such as where it is smallest or changes sign.
docs.title: Mathematical functions and tables of values
